Countenance
KOWN-tuh-nints
noun (KJV vocabulary / covenant theology / anthropology)
Old French contenance (bearing, demeanor, manner), from Latin continentia (self-restraint, bearing, containment), from continere (to hold together, contain); in the Authorized Version, the word renders Hebrew pānīm (פָּנִים, face, presence, person — a plural of majesty) and carries both the literal meaning of facial expression and the theological meaning of God's personal attention and favor directed toward someone.

Biblical Definition

“Countenance” is the Authorized Version's primary word for the face as the bearer of personal expression, divine favor, and covenant attention. Its most solemn theological use is in the Aaronic blessing: “The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace.” (Num 6:26). Here the Hebrew pānīm (face) is translated “countenance” to capture not merely the physical face but the directed, personal, favorable attention of the covenant God — the face turned toward rather than away.

In its negative register, the fallen countenance names the soul in sin: “But unto Cain and to his offering he had not respect. And Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell.” (Gen 4:5). The drooping face is not merely an emotional signal; it is the outward index of the inward state of a man turned away from God. Proverbs captures the opposite: “A merry heart makes a cheerful countenance” (Prov 15:13). The face reveals the condition of the soul — and in the biblical account, the soul's condition is always a spiritual one, shaped by its relationship to the Lord.

The psalmist pleads: “There be many that say, Who will shew us any good? LORD, lift thou up the light of thy countenance upon us.” (Ps 4:6), echoing the Aaronic blessing and grounding all human flourishing in the divine face turned favorably toward its covenant people. The countenance of God is not a metaphor but the personal attention and favor of the God who is Person, not principle.

Webster 1828 Definition

COUNTENANCE: the face as the bearer of personal expression and divine favor; in biblical theology, especially the directed, favorable attention of the covenant God toward His people — as in the Aaronic blessing (Num 6:25–26) — and the outward index of the soul's inward condition.

expand to see more

COUNTENANCE, noun. The face; the features of the face; especially the expression, look, or cast of the face as indicating the condition of the mind.

From Old French contenance (bearing, demeanor), from Latin continentia (self-restraint, manner); the face as the containing surface of personal character.

Webster 1828: “The human face; the features of the face, or the face itself… More particularly, the look, the expression of the face; the air, manner, appearance.”

In biblical usage, “countenance” translates Hebrew pānīm (face/presence) and carries theological weight beyond the physical: God's countenance toward His people is His covenantal attention and favor (Num 6:26); a fallen countenance (Gen 4:5) announces spiritual alienation.

Key Scripture

Gen 4:5 — "But unto Cain and to his offering he had not respect. And Cain was very wroth, and his countenance fell."

Num 6:26 — "The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace."

Ps 4:6 — "There be many that say, Who will shew us any good? LORD, lift thou up the light of thy countenance upon us."

Prov 15:13 — "A merry heart maketh a cheerful countenance: but by sorrow of the heart the spirit is broken."

Modern Corruption

The replacement of “countenance” with the flat modern “face” in contemporary translations strips the word of its covenantal dimension — the directed personal attention of the living God. A subtler corruption psychologizes the divine countenance into an emotional metaphor, losing the objective covenantal reality the Aaronic blessing pronounces over God's people.

expand to see more

Modern translations replace “countenance” with “face” (a legitimate lexical choice) and thereby lose the word's implication of directed personal attention. The Aaronic blessing's “lift up His countenance” (Num 6:26) is not saying that God has a face — a bare physical fact — but that God's personal, covenantal attention is turned favorably toward the recipient. “Face” can be anatomical; “countenance” is always personal. The covenantal weight of the third blessing in the Aaronic triad — peace as the fruit of God's favoring countenance — is diminished when the distinctive term is replaced by a generic anatomical word.

A theological corruption accompanies the lexical one: modern evangelical culture interprets God's “face” or “countenance” as primarily an emotional metaphor for divine approval or disapproval, detached from the objective covenantal act the blessing declares. But the Aaronic blessing is a priestly pronouncement, not a feeling report: the priest speaks the word of God over the congregation, and God Himself covenants to bless (Num 6:27 — “so they shall put My name on the children of Israel, and I will bless them”). The countenance that is “lifted up” is not merely experienced; it is objectively declared and objectively given.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Old French and Latin roots conveying bearing and personal demeanor; in biblical use renders Hebrew pānīm (face/presence), giving the English word covenantal weight that the simple “face” does not carry.

expand to see more

Latin continentia — bearing, self-containment, manner; from continere (to hold together); the face as the surface that “contains” and expresses the inner person

Old French contenance — bearing, demeanor, manner of conduct; entered Middle English carrying the idea of the face as the outward index of inner character

Hebrew pānīm (פָּנִים) — face, presence, person; a plural of majesty rendered “countenance” in theologically charged contexts; God's pānīm toward His people is His covenantal presence and favor (Num 6:25–26; Ps 4:6; Ps 80:3)

The “lifting up” of God's countenance (nāsā' pānīm) is a technical covenantal phrase for God's favorable turning toward a petitioner — the opposite of “hiding the face” (Ps 13:1; Isa 54:8), which signals covenantal withdrawal

Usage

"The Aaronic blessing (Num 6:24–26) structures a threefold declaration: the LORD will bless and keep (general provision); the LORD will make His face shine (gracious illumination); the LORD will lift up His countenance (personal, directed favor) and give peace (shālōm). The third element names peace as the fruit of God's attentive, covenanting face. The Reformed tradition has long preached the Aaronic blessing as a New Covenant reality fulfilled in Christ, through whom God's countenance is favorable toward His people without qualification."

"Calvin's commentary on Gen 4:5 treats Cain's fallen countenance as diagnostic: the outward drooping face is not merely sadness but spiritual alienation manifesting bodily. Calvin notes that the face, in Scripture's anthropology, does not merely reflect what is inside; it is itself part of the moral testimony of the person before God. A man whose face falls in anger at God's righteous verdict is already moving toward fratricide — the face predicts the act."

"The psalms of divine hiding — “How long wilt thou forget me, O LORD? For ever? How long wilt thou hide thy face from me?” (Ps 13:1 KJV) — treat the hidden countenance as covenantal distress. The Lord's hidden face is not God's absence (He is omnipresent) but the withdrawal of conscious covenant communion — the sense that God's favoring attention has turned away. The cry of desolation in Ps 13 is precisely a cry for the restoration of the countenance of Num 6:26. The two poles — the lifted-up countenance and the hidden face — map the range of the soul's experience before God."
